sessions.description: Developer asks conceptual questions about git. No file access, no shell commands. Tests whether 23 tool schemas make sense for pure knowledge queries.

turns.user_input: explain the difference between git merge and git rebase

messages.content: explain the difference between git merge and git rebase

turns.llm_output:
Both integrate changes from one branch into another, but differently:

**git merge** creates a new merge commit that has two parents, preserving the full history of both branches. Safe, non-destructive, but creates a more complex history graph.

**git rebase** moves your commits to the tip of the target branch, rewriting commit hashes. Creates a linear history that's easier to read, but rewrites history — dangerous on shared branches.

Rule of thumb: merge for shared branches (main, develop), rebase for local cleanup before pushing.

analysis.insight: 14-token question, 7500 tokens of context. This is pure knowledge — a stripped system prompt with no tools would answer identically. Tool schemas contribute 0 value here.

turns.user_input: when exactly should I never use rebase
turns.llm_output: Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared remote branch that others have pulled. Rebasing rewrites commit hashes — anyone with the old commits will have a diverged history. The rule: if someone else might have based work on it, don't rebase it.

analysis.insight: Still 0 tools used. History growing. 23 Cron, Worktree, TaskCreate tools sitting idle.

turns.user_input: what about interactive rebase for squashing commits
turns.llm_output: Interactive rebase (`git rebase -i HEAD~N`) lets you squash, reorder, edit, or drop the last N commits before pushing. Safe to use as long as you haven't pushed those commits yet. Squashing is great for cleaning up 'WIP' commit chains into one clean commit.

analysis.insight: 3-turn git Q&A. Every answer came from training data. Zero tools needed. The 4400-token tool schema block was entirely decorative. A system prompt trim + no tools would save ~52% of total tokens with identical output quality.

This is a Django views file handling authentication and user management. Key sections:

**Utilities (lines 401-500)**: Permission decorators, rate limiting helpers, response formatters.

turns.user_input: what are the security risks in the auth section

gateway_payload.messages: [T1 user (~4500 tokens) + T1 assistant (~300 tokens) = ~4800 tokens history + T2 user]

turns.llm_output:
Three risks in the auth section:
1. **Password reset token not rate-limited** (line 67) — an attacker can spam reset emails
2. **JWT secret hardcoded in settings.py reference** (line 89) — should be env var
3. **No brute-force protection on login** (line 23) — no lockout or exponential backoff

The soft-delete pattern (line 241) also means deleted users' tokens remain valid until expiry — worth checking your token cleanup job.

analysis.insight: T2: history (4820) has now overtaken tool schemas (4400) as the #2 cost. The large T1 paste lives in history forever. By T3, history would be ~10000 tokens, becoming the dominant cost.
